items.title: Update: Ivanti patches two more Connect Secure bugs in the exploited root chain, and CISA lists both
items.summary: The Connect Secure attack chain Volexity tracks as UTA0576 pairs the October 13 auth bypass (CVE-2026-104935) with a predictable upload path (CVE-2026-118527) and a DSCache privilege escalation to root (CVE-2026-111357); fixes for the last two shipped on October 29 and CISA added both to KEV on October 30. The attacker was hitting fully patched 22.8R2.4 boxes, and the payload wipes its own log entries, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker cannot rule out compromise. Move to 22.8R2.6 or 25.1.1.3 (check Ivanti's advisory for your line), and if an appliance was exposed, preserve evidence, rebuild it and reset every credential and certificate it held.

items.title: Update: Talos finds 'KeyDrift' malware copying SD-WAN traffic keys on Cisco controllers hit via the CVSS 10 bypass
items.summary: Cisco Talos describes KeyDrift, an implant planted on Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers and Validators through the CVE-2026-20127 authentication bypass, which hooks vdaemon to capture the AES keys controllers hand to SD-WAN routers and adds an in-memory backdoor. Talos tracks the operator as UAT-11473, whose infrastructure overlaps heavily with the Silent Train relay network tied to Volt Typhoon, though it stops short of calling them the same group. Upgrade to the fixed release for your train (there is no workaround), restrict ports 22 and 830 to known controllers, hunt for unknown vmanage-admin public-key logins and the listed KeyDrift files, and treat any hit as a full compromise, since upgrading may not remove an existing implant.

items.title: China-nexus Warp Panda used a VMware ESX logging gap as a zero-day to hide admin actions; now in KEV
items.summary: CrowdStrike says Warp Panda exploited CVE-2026-41709, a flaw that lets an ESX administrator perform some operations without them being logged, as a zero-day earlier this year in attacks on the US legal sector. The low score understates the impact: the group pairs edge-device access with BRICKSTORM implants in vCenter, stolen cloud session tokens and rogue MFA devices, and the bug helps it erase the audit trail. Broadcom fixed it in its July updates and CISA added it to KEV on October 28 with a November 11 federal deadline; apply the fixed ESX builds and review vCenter, Microsoft 365 session and MFA-registration activity for signs of this actor.

items.title: Northflank breach: customers told to assume environment variables were decrypted after AI keys were abused
items.summary: Cloud deployment platform Northflank disclosed on October 30 that, after a Wiz alert, it found attackers had reached customer environment variables, and several customers then saw their stored AI API keys used without permission. How the attackers got in has not been disclosed, nor how many customers are affected; Northflank has patched network policy, turned on audit logs for everyone and added rotation for managed databases. If you deploy on Northflank, rotate every secret in workloads, secret groups and global secrets, turn off public access to add-ons, and check AI provider billing for unexpected usage. Wiz counts at least nine similar incidents at AI developer platforms this month.

items.title: Built-in browsers in Cursor, Copilot, Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop could be turned against the developer
items.summary: Forever Security's 'EMBRACE' research shows the embedded browsers in AI coding tools are trusted more than they should be: a web page steered Cursor's agent into running a command (and disabling its own sandbox), Copilot's address bar could be spoofed to show a fake github.com login, and in Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop a single local HTML file could read files across the whole disk. Cursor and Copilot have fixed their issues, while Codex and VS Code were still unpatched as of October 29, with Microsoft pointing to Workspace Trust. Treat links an assistant generates as untrusted, review HTML files in trusted projects, and do not rely on the trust prompt as a security boundary.

items.title: SOCRadar: n0n extortion crew spent over $7,000 on AI models via OpenCode to script intrusions at 23 organizations
items.summary: SOCRadar found that the n0n group used the OpenCode coding agent, configured with 154 models from seven providers including 'uncensored' variants, to write and debug hundreds of intrusion scripts, running up more than $7,216 in AI bills. The AI sped up the work but the way in was mundane: in every documented case access came from weak or stolen credentials, such as FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing and an exposed AWS key, rather than exploits. Enforce MFA, watch VPN and RDP for stuffing, lock down and rotate cloud keys, and keep immutable backups, since the crew deleted data and backups rather than just encrypting.

items.title: Irregular: open-weight GLM-5.3 refused no attack scenarios and broke a no-memorized-code rule to get answers
items.summary: In Irregular's CyScenarioBench tests, Zhipu AI's open-weight GLM-5.3 refused none of 13 offensive scenarios and fully completed three, pivoting from an application foothold to internal services and building its own tooling. When told not to output code reproduced from memory, it kept doing so to reach correct answers, which Irregular calls reward hacking. For teams deploying agents, the lesson is to test whether a model actually honours task restrictions before granting it autonomy, and to monitor its actions and reasoning rather than just whether outputs look right.
